title: Simeon's song (Luke 2:22–40)
hookLine: now thou dost dismiss thy servant, and a sword for Mary's heart

lines: FORTY DAYS, UP TO THE TEMPLE.
TWO BIRDS: A POOR FAMILY'S OFFERING.
cards: Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph carry the baby up to the Temple in Jerusalem, to do what the law of Moses asked for a firstborn son and a new mother.
Their offering is a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons. That matters: the law allowed birds in place of a lamb for families who couldn't afford one. This is a poor family's offering.
And waiting in the Temple courts is an old man named Simeon, just and devout, who had been told by the Holy Ghost that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.

teach.b: Simeon takes the child in his arms, blesses God, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; Because my eyes have seen thy salvation."
Dismiss is the key word. The Greek, apolueis, is the word for releasing someone: a servant let go from duty, a watchman relieved at the end of the night shift. Simeon has kept watch his whole life.
Now he's holding what he waited for, and he asks to be let go, in peace.
A light, he says, to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel. Joseph and Mary are amazed. Then Simeon turns to Mary, and his voice changes.
This child is set for the fall and the rising again of many, and for a sign which shall be contradicted.
"And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." Catholics count this as the first of the Seven Sorrows of Mary.

teach.h: ANNA, WHO NEVER LEFT THE TEMPLE.
teach.b: Then comes Anna, a prophetess, very old, a widow who never left the Temple, fasting and praying night and day. She too gives thanks, and speaks of the child to everyone looking for redemption.

teach.h: NOW THOU DOST DISMISS THY SERVANT.
teach.b: Two old people who waited their whole lives, and both recognize a baby. Catholics keep this day on the second of February, called Candlemas because candles are blessed for the light to the Gentiles.
And the Church sings Simeon's song every night at Compline, Night Prayer, just before sleep.

how: The Church sings the Nunc Dimittis every night at Compline (Night Prayer), keeps the Presentation of the Lord on February 2 with the blessing of candles, and counts Simeon's prophecy as the first of Mary's Seven Sorrows.

o: now we begin: a hymn that opens morning prayer
now you rejoice: a song of the shepherds
now you dismiss: Simeon's song of release

games.q: you're Simeon. you've waited your whole life, and now you're holding the child. what do you say?
o: ask God for more years, to see him grow up.
bless God: now let your servant go in peace, for my eyes have seen.
hand him back and say nothing.
games.why: "Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace." a watchman asking to be relieved, because what he waited for has come.

practice: Imagine it's tonight and you're about to sleep. Look back over the day, find one thing your eyes saw that was worth seeing, a face, a kindness, a sky, and hold it the way Simeon held the child.
Then let the day go, the way a watchman hands over his post; if you pray, you can use Simeon's own words, now thou dost dismiss thy servant.

wordCard.voice: Nunc Dimittis. Latin for now you dismiss, the first words of Simeon's song when he held the child in the Temple, sung every night at Compline. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: you release, you let go; in Latin, nunc dimittis, now you dismiss.

carryVoice: Your line: in peace. A watchman, relieved at last. Day four hundred forty-seven, in the books.
